title: Ethanol Consumption During Rich-to-Lean Transitions of Food Reinforcement: Manipulation of Ethanol Delivery Mode in the Absence of a Sucrose Fade
abstract: Abstract Previous research in our laboratory demonstrated that transitions from rich-to-lean food reinforcers engender oral ethanol (EtOH) consumption in rats when EtOH was freely available and previously presented in a sucrose solution. Here, we determined whether shifts in food-reward context would establish EtOH consumption in the absence of a sucrose fade and when access was contingent upon a lever press. Six food-restricted male Long-Evans rats lever pressed on a two-component multiple fixed-ratio, fixed-ratio (FR FR) schedule with signaled rich (3 or 4 pellets; lower FR) and lean (1 pellet; higher FR) components. Four transitions between food reinforcers were arranged: lean-to-lean, lean-to-rich, rich-to-rich, and rich-to-lean. After establishing a baseline, an EtOH solution (20% v/v) was made freely available during the session in a bottle. Licks were recorded and sorted by food transition type. After five sessions, the bottle was removed, and rats could produce 0.1-cc, 5-s EtOH (20% v/v) deliveries via a dipper by pressing (FR 1) a concurrently available second lever. Five subsequent extinction sessions were conducted under lever-press conditions using tap water. The schedule of food reinforcement occasioned moderate levels of EtOH consumption, with increased consumption during lean components, and particularly during the rich-to-lean transition. Most rats consumed more EtOH when it was freely available in a bottle, but this difference was not statistically significant. Lever press responding for fluid decreased during extinction but occurred at higher rates in the rich-to-lean transition. Overall, the results demonstrate that rats acquired EtOH consumption in the absence of a sucrose fade, including when a lever press was required to produce it, under transition-type control.
